title: Act III, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: In the hot afternoon Tybalt seeks Romeo. Romeo, newly married to Tybalt's cousin, refuses to fight. Mercutio fights Tybalt; Romeo steps between them and Tybalt wounds Mercutio under Romeo's arm. Mercutio dies cursing both houses. Romeo kills Tybalt and flees. The Prince banishes Romeo.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Act III, Scene I”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: In the hot afternoon Tybalt seeks Romeo. Romeo, newly married to Tybalt's cousin, refuses to fight. Mercutio fights Tybalt; Romeo steps between them and Tybalt wounds Mercutio under Romeo's arm. Mercutio dies cursing both houses. Romeo kills Tybalt and flees. The Prince banishes Romeo.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Mercutio is fatally wounded and Romeo kills Tybalt on stage. Focus on choices and the honour code, not the swordplay. Alcohol: period drinking appears as social custom (wine at feasts, toasts or 'healths') and as a restorative (aqua vitae, i.e. brandy or spirits). Name it plainly; don't glamorize it. Mercutio mocks a brawler who picks fights 'by the operation of the second cup'.
